---
title: "Conditional probability"
---

The joint probability $\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40$ tells us how much of the full pronoun probability belongs to forms that are both plural and accusative. A different linguistic question asks: among plural forms, how much of the probability belongs to accusative forms?

The phrase *among plural forms* changes the reference set. We no longer compare the plural accusative mass with the entire sample space. We compare it with the plural event.

This restricted comparison is a [**conditional probability**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). We write

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
$$

and read the expression as “the probability of $A$ given $P$.” The event to the right of the vertical bar states the condition. The event to the left states what we want to measure within that condition.

## Rescale the plural event

The plural event contains two outcomes:

$$
P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
$$

Their original probabilities are $.10$ and $.40$. Those values sum to $.50$, because the plural event receives half of the mass in the full space.

| plural outcome | probability in $\Omega_4$ | probability within $P$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| *they* | $.10$ | $.10/.50=.20$ |
| *them* | $.40$ | $.40/.50=.80$ |

Dividing each plural probability by $.50$ makes the two restricted values sum to one. Within the plural event, *them* receives probability $.80$. Since *them* is the only plural accusative outcome,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80.
$$

## Derive the definition

The part of $P$ that also belongs to $A$ is the intersection

$$
A\cap P=\{\textit{them}\}.
$$

Its original probability is $.40$. The full conditioning event has probability $.50$. Dividing the relevant part by the conditioning whole gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)}{\mathbb{P}(P)}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.50}\\
&=.80.
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, for $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

The numerator finds the part of the condition where $B$ also occurs. The denominator rescales that part relative to all mass in the condition.

This rescaling makes the conditioning event certain within itself:

$$
\mathbb{P}(C\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\cap C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=1.
$$

## Reverse the condition

Now ask for the probability of plurality among accusative forms. The numerator is still the same intersection, since $P\cap A=A\cap P$. The denominator changes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)}{\mathbb{P}(A)}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.70}\\
&\approx .57.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80$, while $\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\approx.57$. The two expressions use the same overlap but different reference events.

Base R makes the denominator visible.

```{r}
#| eval: false
p_plural_and_acc <- .40
p_plural <- .50
p_acc <- .70

p_acc_given_plural <- p_plural_and_acc / p_plural
p_plural_given_acc <- p_plural_and_acc / p_acc

c(p_acc_given_plural, p_plural_given_acc)
```

The output is `.8` and approximately `.571`.

## Why the condition must have positive probability

If $\mathbb{P}(C)=0$, the original measure places no mass inside $C$ to rescale. The problem is not only arithmetic division by zero. This definition cannot construct a within $C$ probability measure from an event that has no mass.

We will later encounter settings in which conditioning on exact continuous values requires a more careful construction. Nothing from those settings is needed for the finite event calculation here.

## A common failure: transposing conditional probabilities

Swapping the target event and conditioning event transposes the conditional probability. A corpus may show that most passive clauses contain an animate subject. This is a claim about

$$
\mathbb{P}(\text{animate subject}\mid\text{passive}).
$$

It does not by itself show that most clauses with animate subjects are passive, which concerns the reversed conditional.

The safest reading procedure is verbal: read the expression from the condition outward. First restrict to the event on the right of the bar. Then ask what portion also belongs to the event on the left.

## Check your understanding

1. Compute $\mathbb{P}(A^c\mid P)$ from the table and verify that it sums with $\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)$ to one.
2. Compute $\mathbb{P}(P\mid A^c)$ and describe the reference event in words.
3. Explain why $\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)$ and $\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)$ share a numerator but need not be equal.
4. Give a linguistic pair of events for which reversing the condition changes the scientific question.

Conditional probability turns an overlap and a reference event into a probability within the conditioning event. The [next page](probability-factorization.qmd) rearranges this definition to obtain the product rule.
